results.name: large_example_multiple_contrast
results.description: Among targets >=10 from every example and sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate for targets that are multiples only of an example >=13 (no example 2-12 divides them; e.g. 94 after 47) minus yes-rate for targets that are not multiples, divisors or factor-kin of any example; observed < null means the model's size-independent multiples route over-credits multiples of large examples (people's multiple route is a times-table effect for small numbers), observed > null means it under-credits them.
results.code:
# name: large_example_multiple_contrast
# description: Among targets >=10 from every example and sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate for targets that are multiples only of an example >=13 (no example 2-12 divides them; e.g. 94 after 47) minus yes-rate for targets that are not multiples, divisors or factor-kin of any example; observed < null means the model's size-independent multiples route over-credits multiples of large examples (people's multiple route is a times-table effect for small numbers), observed > null means it under-credits them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    nodig = ~((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    g = np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int))
    kin = (pres & (g >= 3)).any(1)

    small = pres & (e1 >= 2) & (e1 <= 12) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)
    large = pres & (e1 >= 13) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)
    base = (d >= 10) & nodig
    a = base & large.any(1) & ~small.any(1)
    b = base & ~mult & ~divi & ~kin
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: far_unrelated_set_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across sets (with >=9 such trials) of the yes-rate for "unrelated" targets (>=15 from every example, sharing no example's final digit, not a multiple/divisor/factor-kin of any example); observed > null means sets differ in how broadly people generalize to unrelated numbers more than the model's stimulus-driven predictions allow (set-level breadth heterogeneity it under-produces), observed < null means less.

    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    nodig = ~((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    g = np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int))

    gr = s.groupby("s")["r"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    gr = gr[gr["size"] >= 9]
    if len(gr) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(gr["mean"].std())

results.name: set_size_mid_distance_contrast
results.description: Among targets 3-12 from the nearest example that share no example's final digit and are not multiples or divisors of any example, yes-rate in one-example sets minus yes-rate in three- or four-example sets; summed similarity makes the model expect more generalization with more examples, so observed > null means people narrow with more examples (size-principle tightening) more than the model predicts, observed < null means they broaden more.

    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    nodig = ~((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    g = np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int))

    base = (d >= 3) & (d <= 12) & nodig & ~mult & ~divi
    a, b = base & (n == 1), base & (n >= 3)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: trial_position_yes_drift
results.description: Yes-rate on trials in the later half of the session (trial_index above the median) minus yes-rate on the earlier half; the model has no time dependence, so observed > null means people become more liberal as the session goes on (and observed < null more conservative), a drift the stationary model fails to produce.

results.name: decade_match_near_contrast
results.description: Among targets 2-9 away from the nearest example that share no example's final digit and are not multiples of any example, yes-rate for targets in the same decade (same tens digit) as some example minus those in no example's decade; observed > null means people use categorical decade membership beyond the model's linear magnitude distance (model under-produces same-decade generalization), observed < null means decade boundaries matter less than the model's distance implies.

    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    nodig = ~((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e, 10)) & pres).any(1)

    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0

results.name: prime_target_in_prime_set_contrast
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all primes, yes-rate for prime targets minus yes-rate for odd non-prime targets (target not itself an example); observed > null means people induce a "prime numbers" rule that the similarity model (no primality dimension) under-produces, observed < null means primes are over-endorsed by the model.
results.code:
# name: prime_target_in_prime_set_contrast
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all primes, yes-rate for prime targets minus yes-rate for odd non-prime targets (target not itself an example); observed > null means people induce a "prime numbers" rule that the similarity model (no primality dimension) under-produces, observed < null means primes are over-endorsed by the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    nodig = ~((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    g = np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int))
    kin = (pres & (g >= 3)).any(1)

    primes = np.array([p for p in range(2, 101) if all(p % q for q in range(2, p))], dtype=float)
    exz = np.where(pres, ex, 2.0)
    allp = np.isin(exz, primes).all(1) & (n >= 2)
    isex = (pres & (t == e)).any(1)
    tp = np.isin(t1, primes)
    a = allp & tp & ~isex
    b = allp & ~tp & (np.mod(t1, 2) == 1) & ~isex
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
results.description: In sets with >=2 examples, among targets within 6 of exactly one example (and >6 from all others), not equal to it, yes-rate when that nearby example is the first shown minus when it is the last shown; the model weights all examples equally, so observed > null means a primacy effect (first example anchors the concept) and observed < null a recency effect the model misses.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
# description: In sets with >=2 examples, among targets within 6 of exactly one example (and >6 from all others), not equal to it, yes-rate when that nearby example is the first shown minus when it is the last shown; the model weights all examples equally, so observed > null means a primacy effect (first example anchors the concept) and observed < null a recency effect the model misses.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    nodig = ~((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    g = np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int))
    kin = (pres & (g >= 3)).any(1)

    near = pres & (np.abs(t - e) <= 6) & (t != e)
    one = near.sum(1) == 1
    isex = (pres & (t == e)).any(1)
    idx = np.argmax(near, axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & one & ~isex
    a = base & (idx == 0)
    b = base & (idx == n - 1)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: multiset_factor_kin_contrast
